clue.text: Running blues? hardly!

parts.note: dyes that bleed in the wash are said to run; blues are colours, and ones that hardly run are dyes fixed so they never leak

explanation.surface: A doubtful remark about whether blue dye bleeds, or blue-shirted athletes are really running.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Running' looks like athletics and 'blues' like sportsmen or sadness, but it is laundry: colour that runs in the wash.
explanation.definitionFit: Dye described as fast stays put in washing, so blues that hardly run are colourfast hues.

clue.text: A school-friend in no casual way

parts.note: a form is a class or year group in a British school
an ally is a friend or supporter

explanation.surface: Someone describes a classmate's stiff, unrelaxed manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting in no casual way is acting with ceremony and correctness, the adverb's sense.

clue.text: Jock might find it fishy for Bob to retaliate thus !

definitions.text: Jock might find it fishy for Bob to retaliate thus !

parts.words: Jock might find it fishy for Bob to retaliate thus !
parts.note: a Scot (Jock) telling Bob to hit back would say 'stick 'im back'; the phrase sounds like a small spiny freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A Scotsman is suspicious of the way Bob gets his own back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fishy' seems to mean suspicious, but it means the answer is a fish; 'stick' is to strike, so striking back gives the name in a Scots voice.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase for striking back doubles as the name of a little spined fish of ponds and streams.

clue.text: A light blue label on the tin ?

parts.note: a tin is a can
a tab is a small label or tag

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a pale blue sticker belongs on a tin.
explanation.walkthrough: Cambridge University's colour is light blue, so 'a light blue' is a Cambridge man, written Cantab. Here the definition and the tin sit at opposite ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Cambridge sportsmen wear light blue, so one of them is a Cantab, short for Cantabrigian.

clue.text: In the money I have enjoyed existence!

indicators.note: the money words are put around the 'I have' words, which sit in them

parts.note: L and D, pounds and pence, from old British money (librae and denarii)
taken as written
VE is the contracted 've

explanation.surface: A wealthy person declares they have had a good life.
explanation.walkthrough: British money was once pounds, shillings and pence, £sd, so L and D stand for money; I'VE goes between them.
explanation.definitionFit: To have enjoyed existence is to have been alive, the past tense of the verb meaning to exist.

clue.text: Northerner keeps his coat on

parts.note: an ulster is a long heavy overcoat; a man from Northern Ireland wearing one keeps 'his coat' on in the province's name

explanation.surface: A man from up north refuses to take off his coat.
explanation.walkthrough: An ulster is a heavy overcoat named after the Irish province of Ulster, so the coat is in the man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Northern Ireland, the province called Ulster, is a northerner of that region.

clue.text: One's name is mud, perhaps, with this activity

definitions.text: One's name is mud, perhaps, with this activity

parts.words: One's name is mud, perhaps, with this activity
parts.note: throwing mud at a rival's reputation is the activity, and one's own name becomes mud by doing it

explanation.surface: A warning that some pastime will ruin your reputation.
explanation.walkthrough: The activity is mud-slinging, and the clue's 'mud' supplies the first half of that phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Hurling things, mud included, is the throwing that makes up mud-slinging, the smear campaign.

clue.text: A cutting saying

definitions.meaning: a toothed blade for cutting wood

explanation.definitionFit: The toothed tool cuts timber, and an old adage is also called by the same three-letter word.

clue.text: A 20 for the snow ?

parts.note: 20-across is footwear; this is the long footwear strapped on to travel over snow

explanation.surface: A cross-reference asks what footwear suits snowy weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 20 refers to 20-across, the footwear in the old woman's nursery rhyme; a runner strapped to the foot is footwear for snow.
explanation.definitionFit: A long runner fixed to a boot is worn on the foot for gliding over snow.

clue.text: Proverbially suitable bounds for an auditorium ?

definitions.text: Proverbially suitable bounds for an auditorium ?

parts.words: Proverbially suitable bounds for an auditorium ?
parts.note: the proverb says these boundaries have ears, so they suit a place built for listening

explanation.surface: A question about the ideal boundaries for a concert hall.
explanation.walkthrough: An auditorium is literally a place for hearing, and the proverb 'walls have ears' gives its boundaries hearing too.
explanation.definitionFit: The sides of a room are its bounds, and the saying grants them ears, ideal for a hall of listening.

clue.text: As a rule it's a sound control

indicators.note: the clue's 'sound' says the control word is spoken and heard as another

parts.note: a rein is a strap used to control a horse

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that, generally speaking, a certain restraint is sensible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As a rule' looks like 'usually' and 'sound' like 'sensible', but 'rule' is the definition and 'sound' the homophone signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch's period of rule is the time on the throne, and to rule is to hold sway as sovereign.

clue.text: Showing traces of the solution of salt I give

indicators.note: a solution dissolves salt, and solving here means working the letters of the words that follow into a new order

explanation.surface: A chemistry note about dissolving salt leaving traces behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solution' looks like chemistry with salt, but it signals rearranging SALT I GIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something left only as a remnant or trace of what once existed is vestigial, like a disused organ.

clue.text: It's difficult to find room in hospital after a brief seven days

indicators.note: the hospital room comes after, so it follows the earlier pieces

parts.note: WK is the short form of week
a ward is a room for patients in a hospital

explanation.surface: Getting a hospital bed after only a short week proves a struggle.
explanation.definitionFit: Something hard to handle or deal with is awkward, a synonym of tricky.

clue.text: One of them suggests, fractionally, a little too much to drink

definitions.text: One of them suggests, fractionally, a little too much to drink

parts.words: One of them suggests, fractionally, a little too much to drink
parts.note: the British phrase 'one over the eight' means slightly drunk, and one over eight is a fraction

explanation.surface: A remark that a certain measure hints at being a bit tipsy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One over the eight' is British slang for one drink too many; written as a fraction, one over eight is one of these.
explanation.definitionFit: A fraction with eight as its denominator, one part of a whole cut into eight, is one of these.

clue.text: Producing those mechanical begging-letters?

parts.note: to touch someone is slang for asking them for money, and the mechanical letters come from a typewriter used without looking

explanation.surface: Someone churns out form letters asking for handouts.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'touch' someone for money is to beg a loan, so begging letters are 'touch' letters; typed by a mechanical method, they give the typing skill.
explanation.definitionFit: Typing by feel without looking at the keys is the method, here reread as typing requests for cash.

clue.text: A general's not usually drunk

definitions.meaning: belonging to Robert E., the commander of the Confederate army in the American Civil War
the sediment left at the bottom of a wine bottle or cask

explanation.definitionFit: The Confederate commander's surname with a possessive, and wine dregs, which drinkers leave in the bottle.

clue.text: The instrument gives out a minor hum

indicators.note: gives out suggests the letters of 'a minor hum' being sent out and scattered into new order

explanation.surface: A musical instrument emits a low, minor-key hum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minor' and 'hum' look like music to go with the instrument, but they are the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A small reed organ worked by pedals is a keyboard instrument.

clue.text: Luminous ring seen if the king of beasts descends

indicators.note: in a down clue the second piece comes lower, below the first

parts.note: an is an archaic word for if, as in Shakespeare's 'an it please you'
the lion is called the king of beasts

explanation.surface: A glowing halo appears when the lion comes down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'If' gives the old word AN, and in a down entry THE LION 'descends' by sitting under it.
explanation.definitionFit: A halo or bright spot seen on a cloud opposite the sun is this luminous ring.

clue.text: Like the Gilbertian lover of a silver churn

definitions.text: Like the Gilbertian lover of a silver churn

parts.words: Like the Gilbertian lover of a silver churn
parts.note: in Gilbert and Sullivan's Patience a song tells of a magnet that fell for a silver churn

explanation.surface: A comparison with an odd romantic character from Gilbert's verse.
explanation.walkthrough: The song 'The Magnet and the Churn' from Patience tells of a magnet that ignored the iron around it and loved a silver churn.
explanation.definitionFit: Resembling the lover in the song, which was a magnet, means having attracting power.

clue.text: Support for the principal holiday

parts.note: the head is the principal of a school
a rest is a break or holiday

explanation.surface: Someone backs the school head's well-earned break.
explanation.definitionFit: A cushion that props up the back of the skull, as on a seat, is a support.

clue.text: A meaty dish Silas Wegg would have considered " mellering " ?

parts.words: Silas Wegg would have considered " mellering " ?
parts.note: Silas Wegg, the ballad-selling rogue in Dickens's Our Mutual Friend, speaks in mangled Cockney; the quoted word is his kind of pronunciation

explanation.surface: A Dickens character comments on a savoury dish in his own mangled English.
explanation.walkthrough: The allusion to Silas Wegg's speech is only colour; the solver gets the answer from 'a meaty dish' and crossings.
explanation.definitionFit: Boned meat pressed in its own jelly and served cold is a classic cold-table dish.

clue.text: An old woman's overcrowded home

parts.note: the nursery rhyme 'There was an old woman who lived in a...' says she had so many children she did not know what to do

explanation.surface: An elderly lady's house is packed to bursting.
explanation.walkthrough: The British nursery rhyme's old woman lived in a piece of footwear with too many children.
explanation.definitionFit: In the nursery rhyme the crowded dwelling is a piece of footwear.

clue.text: Think of a number-more than one

parts.words: Think of a number-more than one
parts.note: grammatical number is singular or the other kind, so a number meaning more than one is the grammar term

explanation.surface: A party trick: pick a number, any number bigger than one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Think of a number' looks like a maths trick, but number here is grammar: singular or its opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: The grammatical number for more than one thing is the opposite of singular.

clue.text: As a neck turned sideways

indicators.note: turned suggests twisting the letters of 'a neck' round into a different order

explanation.surface: Someone twists their neck to look sideways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned' looks like the neck turning its head, but it is the anagram signal working on the letters of 'a neck'; 'As' is taken as written.
explanation.definitionFit: To look obliquely, out of the corner of the eye, is to look sideways, the adverb's sense.

clue.text: Large enough for a member when there's drink about

indicators.note: the drink goes about, around the member

parts.note: ale is beer
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: Is a portion big enough for an MP if there's beer around?
explanation.definitionFit: Plenty, sufficient in amount or size, is what large enough means.

clue.text: Transmitted a song in a pipe

indicators.note: the song goes in the pipe, inside it

parts.note: a reed is a pipe, as in a reed instrument
a lay is a song or ballad

explanation.surface: A tune is played on a pipe.
explanation.definitionFit: Passed on from one station to the next is transmitted, as a broadcast is.

clue.text: Drink up like a king !

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the drink word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: lager is a drink

explanation.surface: A toast: drink up and feel like royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drink up' looks like an order to finish your glass, but 'up' reverses LAGER.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingly or befitting a monarch is regal, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Soft, strikingly good child's talk

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, soft
rattling is old British slang for excellent, as in 'a rattling good yarn'

explanation.surface: A child's gentle, delightful chatter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rattling good' is dated British praise, so 'strikingly good' gives RATTLING.
explanation.definitionFit: Babbling chatter, such as a small child makes, is the noun's sense here.

clue.text: It's first on the scene of the accident

definitions.text: It's first on the scene of the accident

parts.words: It's first on the scene of the accident
parts.note: emergency help given before medics arrive is called first ___, so this word comes after 'first'

explanation.surface: A description of whoever arrives first at a crash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' looks like 'earliest to arrive', but it is the word that precedes the answer in the phrase for emergency treatment.
explanation.definitionFit: Help given at once after an accident is first aid, the phrase the clue completes.

clue.text: "Astley, and Sir Marmaduke, and Rupert of the --" (Macaulay)

definitions.text: "Astley, and Sir Marmaduke, and Rupert of the --" (Macaulay)

parts.words: "Astley, and Sir Marmaduke, and Rupert of the --" (Macaulay)
parts.note: a line from Macaulay's poem The Battle of Naseby naming royalist commanders; Prince Rupert was named after the German river region of his birth

explanation.surface: A quotation from Macaulay's Civil War ballad with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Prince Rupert, Charles I's cavalry general, was the son of the Elector Palatine, so he was 'of' the great German river.
explanation.definitionFit: Rupert's title links him to the Palatinate, the German river region that names him in the poem.

clue.text: The last word in trend-setting

indicators.note: the clue says the answer is in the next word, its letters sitting inside it

explanation.surface: A fashion writer calls something the very latest trend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The last word in' looks like 'the latest in fashion', but 'in' signals letters inside trEND-setting.
explanation.definitionFit: A conclusion or finish is the final word of something, its close.

clue.text: Time — limit for a Babylonian journey

definitions.text: Time — limit for a Babylonian journey

parts.words: Time — limit for a Babylonian journey
parts.note: the nursery rhyme asks 'How many miles to Babylon? ... Can I get there by ___?', and answers that you can, and back again

explanation.surface: A question about the deadline for a trip to Babylon.
explanation.walkthrough: The British nursery rhyme 'How many miles to Babylon?' asks whether you can get there by a lamp-lit hour, the time limit.
explanation.definitionFit: Evening, the hour when wax lights are lit, is the time the rhyme sets for reaching Babylon.
